title: Family-led intensive care diaries and post-intensive care syndrome in patients and relatives: a narrative review
abstract: Diaries written during intensive care are offered to help survivors make sense of memory gaps. This narrative review, based on a documented librarian-supported search and reported against SANRA, summarises evidence on diaries written mainly by relatives: effects on post-traumatic stress, anxiety and depression in patients and relatives, harms of reading, and how programmes are delivered. Results and conclusions will be written after charting.
introduction: Post-intensive care syndrome affects survivors and relatives. Diaries are widely used, but clinicians disagree about their benefit, and most studies do not separate family-written from staff-written entries.
methods: Search of three databases and two guideline repositories in October 2026 with a librarian, citation chasing, one screener with a second checker for 20 percent of exclusions, a fixed charting form and thematic synthesis with a table of reported estimates. No pooling.
results: Not yet written. The section will present the flow of records, the charted studies by design and by who wrote the diary, reported estimates for patients and relatives, harms of reading and delivery features.
discussion: The discussion will state what can and cannot be concluded about family-written diaries, give practice points on reading support and equity of offer, and name the evidence that would change the guideline.
limitations: Narrative synthesis with one main reviewer; English-language search; few studies of family-written diaries.
conclusion: To be written after charting; it will be worded by certainty and will not state that diaries prevent post-traumatic stress.
summary: SANRA-structured draft with results left empty until charting is complete.
